newsitem.title: HUNGARY: New NATO entrants to cooperate on fighter deals.
newsitem.headline: New NATO entrants to cooperate on fighter deals.

text.p: Defence ministers of Hungary, Poland and the Czech Republic, the three states invited earlier this week to join NATO, agreed on Saturday to harmonise their future fighter procurement policies.

"We have come to an agreement that we shall have closer cooperation in terms of the development of armed forces, with special attention to procurement of fighter aircrafts," Hungarian Defence Minister Gyorgy Keleti told a news conference, held with his Czech and Polish counterparts.

Hungary wishes to replace its ageing fleet of 30 Soviet MiG-21s which fly alongside the country's 28 more modern MiG-29s, with the world's biggest planemakers lining up for an anticipated deal worth $1 billion.
The Czech Republic intends to buy a similar number of planes, while Poland needs up to 100 multi-purpose fighters.

However, Czech Defence Minister Miloslav Vyborny added that the three have not decided the types of aircraft they would purchase, saying this issue belonged to the competence of governments and parliaments as well.
"It's a very complicated decision for the ministers of defence. It's also the problem of governments, parliaments," Vyborny said, adding that they have not fixed any time schedule either.
Keleti told U.S. Defence Secretary William Cohen, who visited Hungary this week, that it could take Hungary 10 years to upgrade its Soviet-style military to full NATO standards.
Keleti, Vyborny and their Polish counterpart, Stanislaw Dobrzanski, discussed the opportunities to further develop their cooperation in light of their invitation to join NATO.

Prime Ministers of Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic will meet in the southern Polish city of Krakow on August 22 to discuss joint steps on both NATO and European Union integration ahead of accession talks.
Keleti said the three defence ministers, who signed a joint communique, also agreed to maintain cooperation with other eastern European states who do not figure in the first wave of NATO enlargement.

A NATO summit in Madrid this week reassured Slovenia, Romania and the Baltic States that they would be considered seriously in future expansions and pledged that all new democracies had the right to join the defence alliance.
The three defence ministers also agreed to meet in Prague three months from now and in Warsaw three months after that, Keleti said.
